state.misconception_label: Thinks you can find missing values in a given table by treating the row as linear and adding on the difference between the first two values given.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: The equation \( f=3 r^{2}+3 \) is used to find values in the table below. What is the value covered by the star? \begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline\( r \) & \( 1 \) & \( 2 \) & \( 3 \) & \( 4 \) \\ \hline\( f \) & \( 6 \) & \( 15 \) & \( \color{gold}\bigstar \) & \\ \hline \end{tabular}. I got \( 24 \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you have a jar of marbles, and each row represents a different color. If you know the pattern for how many marbles are added each time, you can predict how many marbles of a certain color will be in the jar. In this case, we need to use the equation to find the value covered by the star in the table. Let's think about how the pattern works and apply it to the table.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, I get that we need to use the equation to find the value instead of just adding a difference. But how do I actually use the equation \( f = 3r^2 + 3 \) to find the missing value for \( r = 3 \)? Do I just plug in \( 3 \) for \( r \)?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think of the equation as a recipe for how many marbles are added each time. When you plug in \( r = 3 \), you're essentially following the recipe to find out how many marbles of a certain color will be in the jar at that point. So go ahead and substitute \( r = 3 \) into the equation to find the value covered by the star.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher uses vague marble analogies rather than directly addressing the linear addition misconception, provides minimal cognitive challenge by essentially telling the student what to do, but the student does show some progress by recognizing they need to use the equation rather than add differences.
score.justification_pass2: While the teacher attempts to use a concrete analogy (marbles in a jar), the analogy is vague, doesn't clearly map to the mathematical structure of the quadratic function, and fails to genuinely ground the abstract concept in a meaningful real-world situation that aids understanding.
